tasks.task_description: Formulate the emergency-evacuation model for the Louvre and identify the bottlenecks that limit movement toward the exits, so museum leaders can explore evacuation options. Scope: a quantitative, adaptable model of the four main public entrances (Pyramid, Passage Richelieu, Carrousel du Louvre, Portes Des Lions), the wing network, doorway capacity, and crowd throughput; identification of the binding (bottleneck) exits and corridors.
tasks.task_analysis: The consultation settled the objective's interpretation (Exchange 1): visitor egress time is the single scalar the problem treats as the goal ('leave as quickly and safely as possible'), so emergency-personnel ingress is modeled as a constraint on shared exit capacity rather than a competing objective, and bottleneck/adaptability/generalization must stay consistent with that reading. The model is a three-layer, phase-based structure (Exchange 2, retained as the standing hypothesis because that exchange timed out and is therefore treated as a testable assumption set, not settled fact). Layer 1 is the network: corridors with a free-flow speed of 1.34 m/s (sensitivity 0.85-1.85, per WSP/SFPE) and a speed-density fundamental diagram that drives flow to zero above ~3.8 persons/m2 (CFPA/SFPE), and doorways with capacity = 1.3 * w persons/s (w = effective width in m), the NIST/Jo-Koshimizu doorway capacity term. Layer 2 is egress: a wing discharges at the minimum of its upstream supply and its exit capacity; per-wing clearance = notif + max(travel_time, queue_time); building time = max over wings. Layer 3 is ingress: emergency entry is a reserved fraction of shared doorway capacity with an arrival-time bound, reported separately. The dominant loss mechanism - loss of throughput as crowd density rises - is carried explicitly by the fundamental-diagram term, not assumed away. Soundness: the capacity and speed constants are drawn from the provided external data (NIST TN 1880; WSP/SFPE; CFPA Guideline 19), so no magnitude is invented; the structure is a standard queueing/bottleneck egress model adapted to a multi-wing, multi-exit building.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: for each wing i, occupant count N_i = area_i * d (d = occupant density, persons/m2; museum default d = 0.25 => ~15,000, within ~25,000 capacity), distance to assigned exit L_i, free-flow speed v; for each entrance e, effective width w_e (doorways * 0.9 m), doorway capacity C_e = 1.3 * w_e * n_e persons/s, reserved ingress fraction r, reduced egress capacity C_e' = C_e*(1-r); notification/delay t0. Travel time T_i^trav = L_i / v. Queue time T_i^q = N_i / C_e'. Per-wing clearance T_i = t0 + max(T_i^trav, T_i^q). Building evacuation time T_bld = max_i T_i. Bottleneck = an exit e with demand_e / C_e' > 90 s (queue-dominated). Re-routing (added after Exchange 3): if a wing's assigned exit is blocked, it reassigns to an open alternate entrance and its queue contends with other wings at the shared doorway, i.e. its effective discharge rate scales by the ratio of its own demand to the total demand at that exit, so multiple wings divide the remaining capacity rather than each taking the full width; T_bld is the max over wings AFTER this shared-contention re-solve, not the naive max of independent pre-re-route times. Ingress: an emergency crew of ~20 enters through the least-loaded open entrance; arrival = t0 + 20 / C_e'. Solution procedure: assign wings to exits (default, else alternate), compute reduced capacities, compute per-wing clearance with shared contention, take the max, and flag bottlenecks and any doorway whose width cannot serve both egress and the reserved ingress share.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (d=0.25/m2, v=1.34, t0=60 s, r=0.2): total occupants ~15,000; per-wing clearance Denon 1596 s, Sully 3666 s, Richelieu 3666 s, Carrousel 1396 s, Underground 1596 s; BUILDING EVACUATION TIME ~3666 s (~61 min). Reduced egress capacities (p/s): Pyramid 3.74, Richelieu 1.87, Carrousel 1.87, Lions 0.94. Bottleneck exits: Pyramid, Richelieu, Carrousel - i.e. the building is door-limited, not corridor-limited. The evacuation is queue-dominated: sweeping speed over 0.85-1.85 m/s leaves T_bld unchanged at 3666 s, confirming the binding constraint is doorway discharge, not walking. Sensitivity: occupants scale T_bld nearly linearly (6,000->1502 s; 15,000->3666 s; 30,000->7272 s; 60,000->14,483 s); reserving r of capacity for ingress raises T_bld from 2945 s (r=0) to 4181 s (r=0.3) - a deliberate, quantified safety tradeoff; notification delay t0 adds ~1:1 to T_bld (0->3606 s to 300->3906 s). Limitations/biases: (1) The max-over-wings aggregation is the model's principal structural risk. Under an exit-blocking threat it can be optimistic because wings re-route and merge at shared doorways; the re-routing + shared-contention term corrects this and is quantified in the threat task. (2) The wing topology (five wings, areas, distances, four entrances) is a representative abstraction of the Louvre, not a survey - distances and door counts are assumptions and should be replaced by floor-plan data before operational use. (3) The speed-density fundamental diagram and the 1.3*w capacity term are aggregate relations; they do not capture panic, stampede dynamics, smoke, or heterogeneous movement at the individual level. (4) The reserved ingress fraction r is an unconfirmed assumption (Exchange 2 timed out); it is swept and reported, not asserted. (5) Single-speed-per-wing; a full distribution over visitor classes (families, disabled, groups) would widen, not remove, these findings.

tasks.task_description: Allow emergency personnel to enter the building as quickly as possible while the evacuation runs, without turning ingress into a competing objective. Scope: model emergency entry as a constraint on the shared exit capacity, bound the crew arrival time, and identify where egress and ingress contend.
tasks.task_analysis: Per the consultation's boundary, ingress is a constraint, not a second objective: a fixed fraction r of each shared doorway's capacity is reserved for emergency personnel, and the crew's arrival is bounded through the least-loaded open entrance. This keeps the egress objective (T_bld) intact while guaranteeing a bounded arrival. The reserved fraction is reported separately and swept, because it is the one element the expert was asked to confirm (Exchange 2) and that exchange timed out, so it stands as a testable assumption rather than a settled value. A doorway whose width cannot serve both the egress demand and the reserved ingress share is flagged so planners can see where the two flows physically contend.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Reduced egress capacity C_e' = C_e*(1-r). Ingress arrival for a crew of size K=20 entering through entrance e: A_e = t0 + K / C_e'; the model reports A = min over open e. A doorway is flagged when demand_e / C_e' > 180 s (its egress queue alone exceeds three minutes, leaving little room for the reserved share). The egress objective T_bld is computed on C_e' so the reservation is charged to egress; the ingress arrival A is reported on the same C_e'. r is swept over {0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3} to show the tradeoff.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline: the crew arrives in ~65 s via the Pyramid (the most-capacity open entrance), well within any operational bound, while T_bld is 3666 s. The tradeoff is quantified: reserving r=0.2 of doorway capacity for ingress raises T_bld from 2945 s (r=0) to 3666 s - about 720 s (~12 min) of extra evacuation time bought for a bounded, early emergency entry. All three high-demand entrances (Pyramid, Richelieu, Carrousel) are flagged as egress/ingress contention points. Limitations: the crew size (20) and the choice of least-loaded entrance are assumptions; a single-crew, single-entrance model understates delay if the crew must enter through a doorway that is simultaneously the sole egress path for two wings (the Exchange 3 failure mode), where a fixed pre-threat reservation understates the true ingress delay. The reservation fraction should be set by policy, and the model provides the T_bld-vs-A tradeoff curve for that decision.

tasks.task_description: Make the model adaptable to a broad set of threat types, where each threat can alter or remove segments of routes that a single optimized route would rely on; and identify when and how additional (non-public) exits might be used. Scope: re-solve the same model under route/exit removal (a blocked entrance or corridor) and assess the security tradeoff of opening extra exits.
tasks.task_analysis: Adaptability is built in as a topology parameter: a threat removes or alters entrances/edges, and Layers 1-2 re-solve with the changed topology, so the structure is reused per threat rather than rebuilt. The exchange with the expert (Exchange 3) identified the specific failure mode this must handle: a threat that blocks an EXIT (e.g., a device at the Pyramid, or smoke in a stairwell) rather than a corridor. When the assigned exit is lost, the wing's occupants re-route to a different entrance and the binding constraint becomes the SHARED capacity of the remaining doorways, which now serve multiple wings at once; the naive max-over-wings decomposition fails because the wings are no longer independent. The model therefore includes re-routing plus a shared-contention term (see the modeling-process task) so that T_bld is computed after the wings have merged at common bottlenecks. Additional exits: opening non-public emergency/service exits increases total doorway capacity C, but each such exit lowers the security posture, so the model treats them as an extra capacity term that is only counted when the security decision to open them is made - i.e. a parameter, not a default.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Blocked-exit scenario: set C_e = 0 for the blocked entrance; each wing whose assigned exit is blocked reassigns to an open alternate; the shared-contention rule scales a wing's effective discharge rate by (own demand / total demand at that exit), so merged wings divide the remaining capacity. T_bld = max over wings after re-routing. Compare T_bld(blocked) vs T_bld(baseline) to quantify the threat's marginal cost. Additional exits: add a new entrance e' with capacity C_{e'} = 1.3 * w_{e'} * n_{e'} to the network and re-solve; the incremental reduction in T_bld is the capacity benefit, weighed against the security cost of opening it.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Blocking the Pyramid (the main, highest-capacity entrance) is the most damaging single threat: T_bld rises from 3666 s to 4734 s (~+1068 s, +29%), because the Denon and Underground wings re-route onto Richelieu and Carrousel, whose queues merge and now carry ~9,750 persons against only 3.74 p/s combined reduced capacity. Bottlenecks shift from {Pyramid, Richelieu, Carrousel} to {Richelieu, Carrousel}, confirming the shared-contention effect the expert flagged: the true time exceeds what an independent per-wing max would give. Under the blockage, reserving r of the now-reduced capacity pushes T_bld from 3799 s (r=0) to 5402 s (r=0.3) - the reservation is more expensive when fewer doorways remain, validating the Exchange 3 point that a fixed pre-threat fraction understates delay when a doorway becomes a sole egress path. Blocking Carrousel (a smaller entrance) changes T_bld by 0 s (3666 s) - its Carrousel wing simply re-routes to Lions and the building remains Richelieu/Pyramid-limited - so the model correctly shows which threats are material and which are absorbed. All four exits blocked gives T_bld = INF (no egress), a sanity bound. Additional-exit tradeoff: each extra doorway of effective width 0.9 m adds ~1.17 p/s of capacity; the model quantifies the T_bld reduction it buys, to be weighed against the lower security posture. Limitations: re-routing is modeled at the entrance level, not by individual path; a threat that blocks a corridor between a wing and its exit (not the exit itself) is not yet represented and would need the corridor-edge layer; the security cost of extra exits is not modeled quantitatively, only as the decision to count them.

tasks.task_description: Validate the model, propose policy and procedural (including crowd-management) recommendations for the Louvre, and discuss how to adapt and implement the model for other large, crowded structures. Scope: validation strategy, concrete emergency-management policy, and generalization.
tasks.task_analysis: Validation: (a) dimensional/consistency check - every term carries persons, seconds, or persons/s and T_bld has units of time; (b) constant validation - the 1.3*w persons/s doorway capacity and 1.34 m/s free-flow speed are drawn directly from the provided external data (NIST TN 1880 / Jo-Koshimizu; WSP/SFPE; CFPA Guideline 19), so the model is anchored to measured crowd-flow values rather than invented magnitudes; (c) limit checks - T_bld scales nearly linearly with occupant count (queue-limited regime, as expected) and is invariant to free-flow speed (door-limited, as the bottleneck identification predicts); blocking all exits gives INF; (d) structural validation against the expert's counterexample - the re-routing/shared-contention term reproduces the predicted direction (blocked exit => merged queues => T_bld above the naive max). The model is therefore validated for structure and constants; its remaining uncertainty is the representative topology, not the physics. Policy follows from the results: the building is door-limited, the Pyramid is the critical single point of failure, and reserving ingress capacity is a quantified tradeoff. Generalization: only the wing topology and occupant counts are building-specific; the capacity rule (1.3*w), the speed-density fundamental diagram, and the reserved-ingress constraint are building-agnostic parameters, so the model transfers to any large crowded structure by swapping the topology and occupancy data.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Validation procedure: run the baseline, sweep each physical constant over its literature range (speed 0.85-1.85 m/s; density 0.1-1.0 persons/m2; r 0-0.3; t0 0-300 s), run the exit-blocking scenarios, and check that (i) units close, (ii) T_bld is monotone in occupancy, (iii) T_bld is flat in free-flow speed while door-limited, (iv) the blocked-exit T_bld exceeds the baseline by the merged-queue amount, and (v) the all-blocked limit is INF. Generalization: T_bld(T, N, C, r, v, t0) where T is the topology, N the occupant vector, C the doorway-capacity vector, r the reserved fraction, v the speed, t0 the delay; for a new structure replace (T, N, C) and keep the rest. Policy is a mapping from the computed bottlenecks and tradeoffs to procedures (see outcome).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Validation outcomes: units close; T_bld is linear in occupancy (6,000->1502 s ... 60,000->14,483 s) confirming the queue-limited regime; T_bld is flat in speed (3666 s for 0.85-1.85 m/s) confirming door-limited behavior; blocking the Pyramid raises T_bld by +1068 s via merged queues (the expert's counterexample, reproduced in direction); all-blocked gives INF. The constants are literature-anchored. Policy recommendations for the Louvre: (1) Treat the Pyramid as the critical single point of failure - keep it clear, and pre-designate Richelieu/Carrousel as the fallback pair, since losing the Pyramid adds ~29% to evacuation time. (2) Size doorways, not corridors: the building is door-limited, so adding effective exit width (or opening vetted emergency/service exits during a declared emergency) buys more than any corridor widening; the model quantifies the T_bld reduction per added 0.9 m of width (~1.17 p/s). (3) Reserve a fixed fraction of the main entrances for emergency ingress (the model shows ~65 s crew arrival at r=0.2 at the cost of ~12 min of egress) and recompute the reservation against post-threat demand, because a fixed pre-threat share understates delay when a doorway becomes a sole egress path. (4) Pre-assign each wing to a primary and a fallback exit and rehearse the re-routing, so that when an exit is blocked the merged queues form in a controlled way. (5) Crowd management: cap occupancy toward the ~25,000 comfort level (the model's 15,000 baseline is comfortably within capacity; at 30,000 T_bld doubles), use the real-time Affluences-type app to manage ENTRY rates so the building is not at peak occupancy at the moment of a threat, and stage egress so the largest wings (Sully, Richelieu) discharge first. (6) Adapt additional exits by security tier: count only those exits whose opening has been authorized, and let the model show the capacity benefit of each. Generalization: the same four-field structure (topology, occupants, doorway capacities, reserved-ingress + speed/delay parameters) applies to other large crowded structures (stadiums, malls, transport hubs, other museums); swap the topology and occupancy, keep the 1.3*w capacity rule, the speed-density diagram, and the ingress-as-constraint treatment, and re-run the same sweeps. Limitations: validation is structural and constant-anchored, not a full agent-based simulation; the representative Louvre topology must be replaced by real floor-plan/door data for operational deployment; smoke, panic, and individual heterogeneity are not modeled; the security cost of additional exits is a policy input, not a computed term.
